title: Senior's toolkit: config, secrets and volumes
summary: Generate ConfigMaps and Secrets, read them back, roll pods after a change, and debug claims that never bind.

steps.title: Senior's toolkit: config, secrets and volumes
steps.body: Config bugs are quiet: the pod runs, but with the wrong values. These commands show what the pod really got.

toolkit.what: Generates the YAML for a ConfigMap from real files instead of pasting them by hand. Pipe it to `apply` or save it to Git.
flags: one key per file, named after the file
toolkit.example: kubectl create configmap api-config --from-file=appsettings.json --dry-run=client -o yaml | kubectl apply -f -

toolkit.what: Creates a Secret. The values are only base64-encoded, not encrypted: RBAC and etcd encryption protect them, not the format.
flags: a value on the command line (it lands in shell history; prefer `--from-file` for real secrets)
toolkit.example: kubectl create secret generic db --from-file=password=./db-password.txt -n shop

toolkit.what: Reads one secret value back, to check it is the one you expect.
toolkit.example: kubectl get secret db -n shop -o jsonpath='{.data.password}' | base64 -d

toolkit.what: Prints the environment the container actually started with. Environment variables are read once at start and never update.
flags: or a mounted file, which does update after about a minute (not with `subPath`)
toolkit.example: kubectl exec deploy/api -- env | grep -i connection

toolkit.what: Applies a Kustomize overlay: one base plus small per-environment patches. Its `configMapGenerator` adds a hash to the name, so pods roll automatically when config changes.
flags: print the rendered YAML without applying

toolkit.what: Claims and the volumes they bound to. A claim stuck in `Pending` means no volume could be provided.
The events say why a claim is Pending: no StorageClass, a class that waits for the first pod, or a zone mismatch.
flags: normal: it binds when a pod using it is scheduled
which classes exist and which one is `(default)`

steps.prompt: You changed `LOG_LEVEL` in the `api-config` ConfigMap and ran `kubectl apply`. An hour later the logs are still at `Information`. The pod reads it with `envFrom`. What do you run?
options: Nothing; wait for the kubelet sync
steps.explain: Environment variables are set when the container starts and never change. New pods pick up the new value. Kustomize's `configMapGenerator` avoids this by changing the name on every change.

steps.prompt: Generate a ConfigMap from `appsettings.json` and apply it, without writing the YAML by hand.
steps.code: kubectl create configmap api-config --__1__=appsettings.json --__2__=client -o __3__ | kubectl apply -f -
steps.explain: `--from-file` makes a key named after the file. `--dry-run=client -o yaml` prints the object instead of creating it, so `apply` can create or update it.

steps.prompt: Match the command to its job.
pairs: read one secret value, still base64-encoded
see what the container started with
render an overlay without applying it
find out why a claim is Pending
see which class is the default

steps.prompt: A new Postgres StatefulSet pod sits in `Pending`. `kubectl describe pvc data-postgres-0` ends with: `no persistent volumes available for this claim and no storage class is set`. What fixes it?
options: Set `storageClassName` in the volumeClaimTemplate to a class from `kubectl get storageclass` (or mark one as default)
steps.explain: Without a class there is nothing to provision a volume dynamically. Restarting does not help: the claim will stay Pending until it can bind.

steps.prompt: Does a running pod see the change without a restart?

steps.title: Make it a habit
steps.body: When config looks wrong, check what the pod got (`exec -- env` or `cat` the file), not what you applied. Generate ConfigMaps and Secrets with `--dry-run=client -o yaml` or Kustomize, and roll the Deployment after every change that comes in through environment variables.
